headings.title: Introduction to Nutritional Assessment
headings.content: Nutritional assessment forms a foundational pillar of comprehensive nursing care in various healthcare settings across Nigeria. As nursing students, understanding this concept is vital because the nutritional status of a patient directly impacts their clinical outcomes, rate of healing, length of hospital stay, and overall recovery process. A structured nutritional evaluation helps healthcare professionals identify deficiencies, excesses, or metabolic imbalances early in the course of hospital admission. This introductory phase requires nurses to recognize that nutrition is not merely about feeding a patient, but a clinical science involving the evaluation of nutrient intake, digestion, absorption, and utilization by the body. In resource-constrained environments, early recognition of nutritional issues prevents severe complications, reduces healthcare costs, and optimizes patient outcomes. Furthermore, cultural, economic, and geographic factors heavily influence dietary patterns in Nigeria, making contextualized nutritional evaluation an indispensable skill for every professional nurse. By mastering the fundamentals of nutritional assessment, nurses bridge the gap between clinical intervention and patient recovery, ensuring holistic and individualized care plans for every client.

headings.title: Core Definition and Purpose
headings.content: Nutritional assessment is formally defined as a comprehensive approach used to define nutritional status using medical, nutritional, and medication histories, physical examination, anthropometric measurements, and laboratory data. The core purpose of this evaluation is to accurately identify individuals who are malnourished or at high risk of developing malnutrition, and to gather baseline data needed to design and implement an effective nutritional care plan. For nursing students, it is important to distinguish between nutritional screening and nutritional assessment. While screening is a quick, general process meant to flag potential risks, a nutritional assessment is an in-depth, systematic investigation conducted when a risk is identified. The purpose extends beyond simple weight tracking; it seeks to uncover the root causes of nutritional imbalances, whether they stem from chronic illness, poverty, ignorance, malabsorption syndromes, or increased metabolic demands. By fulfilling these purposes, nurses can collaborate effectively with dietitians and physicians to restore or maintain optimal nutritional health, thereby supporting tissue repair, immune function, and physiological stability in hospitalized and community-dwelling patients alike.

headings.title: The ABCD Approach to Assessment
headings.content: The ABCD approach is a universally recognized, systematic framework used by nurses and healthcare teams to conduct a thorough nutritional assessment. Each letter stands for a distinct category of data collection and evaluation: Anthropometric, Biochemical, Clinical, and Dietary methods. Anthropometric measurements involve non-invasive body composition metrics such as height, weight, Body Mass Index (BMI), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and skinfold thickness, which are especially useful in detecting wasting or obesity. Biochemical assessment utilizes laboratory parameters, including serum albumin, prealbumin, hemoglobin, and electrolyte panels, to provide objective evidence of visceral protein status, anemia, or metabolic stress. Clinical assessment relies on physical examination performed by the nurse to spot external signs of nutrient deficiencies, such as dry skin, brittle hair, glossitis, bleeding gums, or muscle wasting, focusing heavily on tissues with rapid cell turnover. Finally, dietary assessment evaluates the patient's actual food and fluid intake through methods like 24-hour dietary recalls, food frequency questionnaires, and calorie counts. Integrating all four components of the ABCD approach ensures that the nurse does not rely on a single metric, thus providing a holistic, accurate evaluation of the patient's nutritional health.

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Nursing Practice
headings.content: The clinical significance of nutritional assessment in nursing practice cannot be overstated. Nurses are at the frontline of patient care and are often the first to notice subtle changes in a patient's weight, appetite, or physical appearance. A prompt and accurate nutritional assessment holds immense clinical significance because malnutrition is frequently underdiagnosed in hospital settings, leading to hospital-acquired complications like pressure ulcers, delayed wound healing, increased susceptibility to nosocomial infections, and muscle atrophy. By routinely performing nutritional evaluations, nurses contribute directly to patient safety and quality improvement. It allows for the early initiation of nutritional support, whether through oral supplementation, enteral tube feeding, or parenteral nutrition. Furthermore, recognizing nutritional deficits aids in managing chronic conditions common in Nigerian healthcare settings, such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease, where medical therapy is deeply intertwined with dietary compliance. Ultimately, integrating nutritional assessment into daily nursing duties empowers nurses to advocate effectively for their patients, prevent preventable morbidity, and support rapid recovery.

headings.title: Identifying Malnutrition and Nutritional Risk
headings.content: Identifying malnutrition and nutritional risk is a core competency for professional nurses. Malnutrition encompasses both undernutrition—such as wasting, stunting, and underweight—and overnutrition, which leads to overweight and obesity. Nutritional risk refers to the vulnerability of a patient to develop malnutrition due to underlying disease processes, surgical stress, reduced functional capacity, or inadequate nutrient intake. In many Nigerian clinical environments, nurses encounter patients presenting with protein-energy malnutrition (such as kwashiorkor or marasmus in pediatrics) as well as chronic disease-related malnutrition in adults. Identifying these conditions requires looking beyond standard clinical parameters to evaluate recent involuntary weight loss, changes in dietary intake, severity of underlying illness, and functional status. Nurses utilize validated screening tools to quantify this risk upon admission and periodically during hospitalization. Early identification enables the interprofessional healthcare team to implement targeted nutritional interventions before irreversible tissue damage, severe immune suppression, or metabolic failure occurs, thereby safeguarding the patient's prognosis and quality of life.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Nutritional Screening
headings.content: The role of the nurse in nutritional screening is pivotal for bridging the gap between hospital admission and specialized dietary care. Because nurses maintain continuous, 24-hour contact with patients, they are ideally positioned to perform initial nutritional screenings within 24 to 48 hours of admission. This screening process involves utilizing simple, validated tools—such as the Malnutritional Universal Screening Tool (MUST) or the Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS-2002)—to categorize patients into low, medium, or high nutritional risk groups. If a patient is flagged as being at risk during this screening phase, the nurse is responsible for initiating a comprehensive nutritional assessment or making a formal referral to a clinical dietitian or physician. Furthermore, the nurse monitors daily food intake, records meal percentages consumed, tracks weight trends, and evaluates the effectiveness of ongoing nutritional interventions. By actively participating in nutritional screening, nurses ensure that no patient slips through the cracks of the healthcare system, promoting proactive rather than reactive nutritional management in clinical practice.
